titleStmt.title: Comparing the Specification of a Near-Real Time Commanding System Using Statecharts and AADL

analytic.title: Comparing the Specification of a Near-Real Time Commanding System Using Statecharts and AADL

div.p: In this paper, we discuss a case study that was performed to compare pros and cons of formally specified a near real-time commanding system using the Architecture Analysis Description Language (AADL) and Statecharts modeling notations. Five system parameters and project metrics namely reliability, schedulability, performance, usability and, tool support were identified as criteria to compare the two formal techniques.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In recent years, architectural description languages (ADLs) have been proposed as the promising solutions to formally specify a complex system at a higher level of abstraction. The primarily objectives of ADLs, among other things, are to developing faster (time to mark), cheaper (less costly), and better (conformance to quality attributes) software systems.

The success of any mission critical software system, for most parts, depends on the choice of design, faithful implementation of that design, and adequate testing before the system can be deployed. One method of ensuring success for these types of systems is to formally specifying it and proving that failure does not occur, or if it does, how the system should react.

Currently a number of formal techniques have been developed based on a various mathematical theories as their underlying theory [12]. These techniques have been developed to formally specify and analyze software that must perform correctly in critical situations where failure may result in mission compromise, loss of life and/or financial losses. However, in today's world of ever increasing hardware/software conformity, a silver bullet technique which only tests a software system is hardly the adequate tool to verify the system. Thus, there is a need to specify and prove the correctness of a software system as there is a need to prove the reliability and performance of the hardware platform and I/O system the software runs on.

To this end, the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) developed the Avionics Architecture Description Language (AADL) [8], known as the Architecture Analysis Description Language as a means of specifying the hardware and software architecture of embedded systems while imposing system and environmental constraints on the model. The model can then be analyzed for certain desirable properties (e.g., performance). The AADL has been used and developed extensively by private firms such as Rockwell Collins, Honeywell etc. but has only just begun to appear in Academia.

This work yet is another attempt to enumerate the findings of a case study performed to evaluate the AADL by utilizing it to specify a portion of a near real-time commanding system used to command a payload resident on the International Space Station (ISS). The commanding system -used to command the AgCam Imaging System (see next section) -was also specified using more traditional and proven formal specification techniques which could be applied to this problem genre. These techniques included Statecharts and Petri-net and some of their extensions.

div.head: The AgCam Imaging System
div.p: The Agricultural Camera (AgCam) is a multispectral imaging system that was designed and developed at the University Of North Dakota (UND) to be used onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The AgCam sensor has the capability of imaging in two bands, red and near infrared. Data products generated by AgCam as well as those requested by direct end-users will be made available within a two day period. Endusers include farmers, ranchers, foresters, natural resource managers, K-12 teachers, tribal government officials, and others.

The AgCam payload will be operated from the Science Operations Center (SOC) based on the UND campus. The SOC will serve as the central authority controlling, monitoring and maintaining the AgCam payload. The SOC, in the simplest form interacts with users as depicted in Figure 1. End-user image requests coming via the Digital Northern Great Plains (DNGP), will be accepted and processed at the SOC.

Notifications to the end-users will then be generated informing them of the status of their requests. An image request may be approved or denied based on factors such as conflict with previous requests, availability of payload, likelihood of capturing an image at the requested time etc. The SOC will then acquire images for valid requests and deliver image data to DNGP for processing before an image product is delivered to the end user.

div.head: AgCam: Operations
div.p: AgCam operates onboard the ISS with minimal crew intervention. Thus, to ensure reliable autonomous operation, it becomes crucial that the SOC be able to command and monitor the payload in a way that is safe for the crew as well as the system. The SOC must also ensure that there is no loss of data due to missed imaging opportunities or faulty command sequences. The AgCam commanding system collects and processes commands that can be issued to the AgCam payload. If, after validation, these commands are determined to be safe they are uplinked to the payload. The commanding system performs the necessary verifications and informs the operator if a commanding sequence is not valid, safe or possible.

The inherent non-determinism caused due to communication blackouts provides a challenge in building a safe and reliable commanding system. The SOC can directly communicate with the ISS only for approximately 15-20 minutes every three to four hours. Thus before a new communication window arrives, the state of the payload and the state of previously uplinked commands is entirely unknown. For example, consider the following situation:

An image can only be downlinked if it has been acquired, i.e. a downlink command cannot precede an image acquisition command. The SOC uplinks an acquire image command to the payload in one communication window. When the next window arrives, the SOC assumes that the image has been acquired and uplinks the downlink command. Under the command sequence rules, (acquire image must precede downlink) this is a valid command. However, suppose that the ISS crew had an emergency during the time the image was being acquired and the command cancelled. Due to the communication blackout, the SOC has no way of knowing that the image has NOT been acquired. So how will the payload react when it receives the downlink command with no image to downlink?

The above situation is a simplified version of a number of complex situations that might occur. It is thus extremely important that the commanding system be formally verified to handle these situations and not issue invalid commands. Some of the challenges in developing the commanding system and the scenarios it may face during operation are as follows:

• The commands that are uplinked to the payload have to be verified for multiple reasons such as crew safety, NASA restrictions, prevention of loss of science and mission success. It is thus imperative that the system is formally specified and analyzed to check for the validity of each operation.

• The system shall have to react to a number of random events such a loss of communications, unpredicted unavailability of communications, changes to the state of the payload when there is a loss of communications and predicting such changes. • High operator turnover, which will result in relatively inexperienced operators performing commanding duties. The system thus needs to have high fault tolerance and detection to ensure no unsafe state is reached or unsafe command issued.

div.head: Evaluation Criteria
div.p: As is true when comparing any two objects, we must first identify the criterion that will be used to evaluate the objects being compared. The system properties and characteristics necessary for the safe and reliable operation of the AgCam Commanding System (ACS) automatically become the top candidates for evaluation criteria. However, since we have not seen a commanding system specified in AADL in the public domain, we shall also include project metrics and human factors as criteria for the evaluation. Table 1 lists the criteria that will be used to evaluate the formal techniques.

div.head: Related Works
div.p: This work related to some of the extensions of Statecharts [2] and Petri-nets [10] that are directly applicable to real-time and embed systems. An overview of the AADL and its foundations in MetaH [3] developed by Honeywell. MetaH has emerged as the foundation of the SAE AADL and the primary AADL toolset is also presented.

div.head: AADL
div.p: The Architecture Analysis and Design Language were designed by Society of Automotive Engineers to speed up the creation of a formal specification with high levels of assurance in critical systems such as avionics and space-based systems. Systems such as these represent a small class of mission-critical systems that must be fault-tolerant and secure or loss of life or extreme financial repercussions can result. The AADL has the ability to model functional component interfaces as well as nonfunctional aspects of components, such as timing and reliability [7] which can affect the overall reliability of the system. Furthermore, the AADL provides a means to formally describe a real-time system in terms of interacting software components and hardware components [6]. The AADL was developed specifically to model embedded systems that have challenging constraints on resources such as size, weight power etc. Thus, by very definition, the most direct fields of application for the AADL are the realms of avionic systems, flight management systems, and engine and power train control systems, certain medical devices, industrial process control equipment, robotics, and space applications.

The purpose of the AADL is to provide a standard and precise, machine-processable way of modeling the architecture of a embedded, realtime system, such as an avionics system or automotive control system to permit analysis of its performance-critical characteristics. Defining a standard way to describe system components, interfaces, and assemblies facilitates the exchange of engineering data between the multiple organizations and technical disciplines that are invariably involved in an embedded realtime system development effort. A precise and machine-processable way to describe conceptual and runtime architectures provides a framework for system modeling and analysis, facilitates the automation of several development activities, and significantly reduces design and implementation defects [8].
The main elements of AADL consists of 10 component categories that can further be classified as either software or hardware components.
Hardware components are commonly referred to as the execution platform. Figure 2 represents the graphical icons of the 10 categories that are used in the AADL graphical notation.

A component type specifies a functional interface in terms of features, flow specifications, properties. It represents a specification of the component against which other components operate. Implementations of the component are required to satisfy this specification. A system in the AADL consists of software components that are mapped to hardware components. These component interfaces contain ports that allow for communication between components.

A component implementation specifies an internal structure in terms of subcomponents, connections between the features of those subcomponents, flows across a sequence of subcomponents, modes to represent operational states, and properties. Unlike many other languages, the AADL allows multiple implementations to be declared with the same functional interface [8].

The software categories include data, subprograms, threads, thread groups and processes. The execution platform includes the processor, memory, bus and device components. The system represents a hierarchical composition of all components. The main principle of the AADL is to model a system as a composition of components and to further describe these components [6]. The AADL allows for defining components exhibiting concurrent behavior and mapping these components to the hardware components of the system. Data components in the AADL model static data which can be shared by processes, threads and other components. A process running in a protected virtual address space must contain at least one thread . A process can also include thread groups (for concurrency) and data components. Threads are used to represent a schedulable unit of concurrent execution. A thread can be assembled with other threads to form a thread group. The software components are mapped to the execution platform. Threads are mapped to the processor, which is responsible for the scheduling and execution of threads. Memory components consist of randomly accessible physical storage. A bus is used to connect the processor and memory, which can be defined as a communication channel that exchanges data and control among processors, memory, and other external devices. The last hardware component, the devices, represents an interface to an external device. The device component must be attached to the bus.

Moreover, the AADL has several extensions which include features and properties. Features are used to specify how a component can be interfaced with other components to describe the flow of data and control. Properties are then used to represent attributes or other characteristics of a component.

div.head: Results
div.p: The commanding system was specified using Statecharts [2] and AADL [8] and then the model was tested for the criteria given in table 1. I-Logix Rhapsody 6.1 was used to build and execute the Statechart models. An open source add-on to the UNIX based Integrated Development Environment Eclipse [5] called OSATE 1.2.4 was used to build AADL files and then convert them into graphical AADL models that can be executed and analyzed. The results of the analysis follow.

div.head: Reliability
div.p: The Statecharts based model generated good results with same failures that were due to inaccuracies in the model. When these problems with the model were fixed, the Statechart model performed correctly in all scenarios. However, loading a testing scenario and then executing the model each time proved to be cumbersome.

The open source OSATE AADL modeling tool does not yet have a plug-in to perform the kind of reliability analysis that we wish to carry out. However, AADL supports the definition of hardware components along with constraints such as signal timings, expected data packet loss on transmission etc. Although not performed in this case study, we can see that these features will enable us to perform a different kind of analysis. For example, what would happen if a valid command sequence never reached the payload? The software system which validated the sequence cannot is oblivious of this fact and will fail if it does not take it into consideration while validating the next command sequence. We suggest the use of AADL and Statecharts in tandem to complement each other and deliver a near perfect analysis. Model the internal software commanding system behavior with statecharts and model the hardware communication system with AADL and then execute the test scenarios simultaneously on both models.

div.head: Schedulability
div.p: Performing schedulability analysis using Statecharts proved to be challenging as well as very inefficient. The main reason for this can be attributed to the fact that Statecharts inherently do not support any methods for schedulability analysis. Two separate models are needed; one to model the processor and the second to model the software process running on that processor. These models can then be executed together and schedulability analysis performed. However, if at any time the processor is replaced by a different one, we would need to construct an entire new model for the processor and run the analysis again.

On the other hand, AADL gives you the tools to specify the type, speed and multiplicity of the processor(s) you wish to deploy. Thus, on running a schedulability analysis, if one processor proves to be insufficient, then you can simply boost up the speed or replace it with a different one or add a second processor etc. until all processes can be successfully bound to a processor. In case of the ACS, the current command validation algorithm was successfully bound to a Pentium 2.4 GHz processor.

div.head: Performance
div.p: Analyzing the performance of the system presented similar problem as those stated in 5.2 above when trying to carry out the analysis using statecharts. It is difficult if at all possible to attach a number or percentage to the performance of the ACS using Statecharts. When carrying out a similar study using the AADL model, the OSATE environment provided an automated tool that quantified the performance in terms of CPU use/availability as a percentage. Again, optimizing performance would be an easy task to accomplish by changing the number/speeds of processors available to run processes.

div.head: Usability
div.p: Statecharts are an intuitive and comparatively easy technique to learn especially if one some experience with finite state machines. Thus, it is our opinion that the models were fairly easy to construct. However, once the models were constructed, they were very rigid and hence hard to modify.

AADL on the other hand demands a considerable time and effort to grasp the basics and the syntax of the underlying language, MetaH. Once the models have been developed they are relatively easy to modify and analyze because of the tools support.

div.head: Tool Support
div.p: Extensive open source tool support exists for Statecharts. Models can be created using one of these tools and then executed. The capabilities of Statechart tools fall short because of the nature or statechart models. As mentioned before, even if Statechart tools exist to make model construction and analysis easier, the models themselves are very rigid. In today's fast paced development cycles, using such inflexible models would reduce productivity. AADL has tool support that is fast growing. The OSATE 1.2.4, the AADL tool support, used to perform this case study includes MetaH semantic checkers that helped. In simplest form, OSATE can convert MetaH files into graphical AADL models and vice versa automatically. The Eclipse [5] environment in addition offers a unique advantage. It is possible to use built-in Eclipse utilities to transform UML models into AADL models and vice versa. This can be an extremely powerful utility as inexperience persons wishing to harness AADL's analytical power can use UML models to generate equivalent AADL models for analysis.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Even though much of the knowledge in the AADL field today is proprietary, it is fast becoming a language in the public domain. More and more tools will be developed as academic institutions push the growth of AADL from private to the public sector. We have found that one of the most powerful features of AADL is that of layered inter-conversion pf models using Eclipse. Models can be iteratively transformed from one specification to UML [1] and then back to another specification or even code.
